name: Acetaminophen
mechanism: Analgesic and antipyretic acting centrally. The FDA label states the precise mechanism is not established, only that it is thought to be primarily central — it is not an anti-inflammatory and does not affect platelets.
indications: Moderate to severe pain, alongside an opioid
contraindications: Severe hepatic impairment or severe active liver disease
pearls: No effect on platelet aggregation or small-vessel hemostasis — the label is explicit, which is why it is the analgesic of choice when bleeding is a concern
Overdose is hepatotoxic; the ceiling matters more than the single dose
Antipyretics lower a fever driven by the hypothalamus. They do not treat environmental hyperthermia — cool the patient

Prostaglandins hold the kidney’s afferent arterioles open; blocking them drops perfusion in chronic kidney disease and hypovolemia

name: Ketorolac
mechanism: NSAID with analgesic activity. The label describes the mechanism as not completely understood but probably prostaglandin synthetase inhibition, and notes it has no sedative or anxiolytic properties. Peak analgesic effect at 2–3 hours.
indications: Short-term (≤5 days) management of moderately severe acute pain requiring analgesia at the opioid level
contraindications: Active peptic ulcer disease, recent GI bleeding or perforation — or any history of either
Asthma, urticaria or allergic-type reaction after aspirin or another NSAID
pearls: The label carries a Boxed Warning; the GI contraindication covers a past history, not just active bleeding, which is stricter than most NSAIDs

Prostaglandins hold the kidney’s afferent arterioles open; the same renal caution as ibuprofen applies

name: Aspirin
mechanism: The acetyl group binds a serine residue on COX-1, irreversibly inactivating the enzyme. Arachidonic acid can no longer become thromboxane A2, so the platelet cannot aggregate — for its whole 7–10 day lifespan.
indications: Chest pain suggestive of acute coronary syndrome
Reducing risk of death and MI in chronic coronary artery disease
Reducing risk of death and recurrent stroke after ischemic stroke or TIA
contraindications: The syndrome of asthma, rhinitis and nasal polyps — may cause severe urticaria, angioedema or bronchospasm
Active ulcer disease or active bleeding
pearls: Irreversible is the point: the platelet has no nucleus and cannot make new COX-1, so effect lasts the platelet’s lifespan, not the drug’s half-life
The extended-release label carries a Limitation of Use — use immediate-release aspirin where rapid onset is needed, such as acute MI. Chewed, not swallowed whole
Aspirin-sensitive asthma travels with nasal polyps and rhinitis; ask about all three

name: Albuterol
mechanism: Beta-adrenergic agonist. Stimulates adenyl cyclase, raising cyclic AMP inside the cell, which relaxes bronchial smooth muscle. Preferential for beta-2 receptors, the predominant receptor in bronchial smooth muscle.
indications: Relief of bronchospasm in reversible obstructive airway disease (asthma)
contraindications: History of hypersensitivity to any component
pearls: Beta-2 selectivity is preferential, not absolute — the label notes 10–50% of receptors in the human heart are beta-2, which is why tachycardia, tremor and chest tightness follow a dose
Tachydysrhythmia and severe coronary disease are cautions to weigh, not label contraindications
Routinely combined with ipratropium; RI authorises both at AEMT

name: Ipratropium bromide
mechanism: Anticholinergic (parasympatholytic). Antagonises acetylcholine at muscarinic receptors on bronchial smooth muscle, preventing the rise in intracellular calcium that would otherwise constrict the airway. It blocks vagally-mediated reflex bronchoconstriction rather than stimulating relaxation.
indications: Bronchospasm with COPD, including chronic bronchitis and emphysema (the labelled indication is maintenance)
Acute bronchospasm alongside a beta agonist — the prehospital use, authorised at AEMT by the national Scope of Practice Model and by RI
contraindications: Hypersensitivity to ipratropium bromide or any component
Hypersensitivity to atropine or any of its derivatives
pearls: Different lever from albuterol: albuterol pushes the muscle to relax, ipratropium stops the signal telling it to squeeze — which is why they are given together rather than one instead of the other
Minimal cardiac effect compared with a beta agonist; side effects are mostly local — dry mouth, cough
The atropine cross-sensitivity is a contraindication in its own right, worth asking about

name: Oxygen
mechanism: Raises the oxygen available to the blood so tissue can keep making ATP aerobically. It corrects hypoxemia; it does nothing for a patient whose problem is ventilation or perfusion rather than oxygen content.
indications: Hypoxemia from any cause — COPD, pneumonia, severe asthma, heart failure
pearls: Titrate to the patient rather than running high flow by reflex — oxygen corrects hypoxemia, and a patient who is already saturated gains nothing from more of it
Fire risk: no smoking, no flammable material near a patient on oxygen
Secure cylinders upright. A falling tank that loses its valve becomes a projectile
Nasal cannula 1–6 L/min; a nebulizer needs 6–8 L/min to aerosolize properly
